A practice with a hundred old five-star reviews can lose to one that's clearly active this month. Recency and consistency tell the engine you're a safe, current name to hand a patient.

We asked the four big AI engines to recommend a plastic surgeon, and out of three strong practices in the same city, only one name came back.

The gap had nothing to do with skill. The practice that got named had reviews a patient could find, a presence on the directories AI already trusts, and web pages written clearly enough for a machine to quote. The other two did excellent work that mostly lived offline, so the engine had nothing to point at.

It's worth knowing which group you're in before a patient asks.

Your procedure page might look polished to a visitor and still read as almost empty to an AI.

Engines can't pull text out of an image, a slider, or a PDF, so a page that keeps its procedures and credentials in those places gives the machine very little to work with. Move that same information into plain text and the page starts answering the questions patients ask AI.

The build barely changes, but what the engine can see changes a lot.

Your Google Business Profile is one of the first places AI checks when deciding whether to recommend a surgical practice.

A few fields carry most of the weight. The primary category and service list tell the engine what you actually do. Recent reviews show that the practice is active and trusted, and consistent contact details across the web keep you from looking like two separate businesses.

Most profiles have gaps in at least one of these.

The credential is real either way, and the question is whether AI can see it.

When someone asks AI for the best injury attorney nearby, a shortlist appears in seconds, and the way it gets assembled is fairly predictable.

The engine gathers what it can find about local firms from directories like Avvo and Justia, from Google reviews, and from bar and Super Lawyers listings. It favors firms with consistent, complete profiles it can trust, then names a few. If your listings are thin or don't match, you're left off before the searcher ever sees a name.

That's why the number is only useful once you can see the pieces behind it.
